question: A 78-year-old male comes to the physician’s office for a routine check-up. He complains of increased lower extremity swelling, inability to climb the one flight of stairs in his home, and waking up in the middle of the night 2-3 times gasping for breath. He has had to increase the number of pillows on which he sleeps at night. These symptoms started 9 months ago and have been progressing. The doctor starts him on a medication regimen, one of which changes his Starling curve from A to B as shown in the Figure. Which of the following medications is most consistent with this mechanism of action?
analysis: The patient's symptoms suggest heart failure, characterized by fluid retention (lower extremity swelling), exertional dyspnea (inability to climb stairs), and orthopnea (increased pillows at night). The Starling curve represents the relationship between stroke volume and end-diastolic volume. A shift from curve A to B typically indicates an increase in contractility or a decrease in preload. Among the options, furosemide is a diuretic that reduces preload by decreasing fluid volume, which would shift the curve appropriately. Other options like metoprolol and digoxin primarily affect heart rate and contractility, while hydrochlorothiazide and aspirin do not directly relate to the Starling curve changes in this context. Therefore, furosemide is the most consistent with the described mechanism of action.
